caption:
Who actually wrote the Codex Gigas?

It is the largest surviving medieval manuscript in the world: 92 cm long, 50 cm wide, 22 cm thick, 74.8 kg. 310 leaves of vellum, claimed to be made from the skins of 160 donkeys.

It was made in the early 13th century at the Benedictine monastery of Podlažice in Bohemia. Inside is the complete Latin Vulgate Bible, plus Josephus, Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae, the chronicle of Cosmas of Prague, and medical treatises. The records in it stop in 1222.

On folio 290, alone on an otherwise empty page, stands a Devil about 50 cm tall — dark green head, red horns and claws, four fingers on each hand, two red tongues. Facing him is the Kingdom of Heaven. The pages just before him have blackened, because readers kept turning to that picture and exposing them to light.

The legend: a monk sentenced to be walled up alive promised to write, in one night, a book holding all human knowledge. Near midnight he prayed to Lucifer for help. Handwriting analysis does say one scribe wrote the whole book — but over an estimated 20 to 30 years.

Swedish troops took it as war booty in 1648. In the 1697 fire at the Tre Kronor castle in Stockholm it was saved by being thrown out of a window; the vicar Johann Erichsons recorded that it landed on a bystander and injured them.

Still unresolved: twelve of the original 320 leaves were removed. Nobody knows who took them, or what was on them.

Images: the Devil folio in an enhanced CC0 scan, and pages of the Codex Gigas from the Benedictine monastery of Podlažice, now at the National Library of Sweden — public domain.

cards.headline: All Latin — except <y>two Hebrew alphabets</y>
cards.note: They sit on the first page, next to the opening of Genesis. Everything after them is written in Latin.

cards.alt: Manuscript page with Hebrew letters at top left and a red Latin text column right.
